statement: BTS estimates that rising highway construction costs reduced the economic value of IIJA funding by 32 percent from FY 2022 to 2025, with highway construction costs up 63 percent from FY 2021 to 2025.

Overall, highway construction costs grew 63 percent from FY 2021 to 2025 [FHWA n.d.], which has reduced the amount of highway infrastructure that funding recipients can buy.
locator: Summary text, first page of the brief (June 2026)
context: BTS, U.S. DOT, second Trump administration; presented as that administration's analysis. It rests on FHWA's National Highway Construction Cost Index (a measured series). note: I did not reproduce the 32 percent from the index values. The brief's other lines show a different measure: a 63 percent cost rise from FY2021 to 2025 alone implies a larger loss for FY2025 by that formula, so the dossier should say which measure it uses. The brief updates BTS's 2024 brief on a calendar-year basis; this version moved to fiscal years and its embedded PDF title still reads '30%... 2022 to 2024'. Cost index growth slowed to 0.6 percent in FY2025.

note: The 2025 task force report (SRC-3111, Report to the Oregon Legislative Assembly) says the fuels tax is 'extremely inexpensive to collect' because a handful of wholesalers remit almost all of it, and that a road usage charge 'will be comparatively more expensive to administer than the fuels tax'. Utah's projected ratio is EV-MOV-120.

statement: Utah DOT reported that 9,703 vehicles were enrolled in its road usage charge program in July 2025, a 45% increase from July 2024.
anchor: IN JUL 2025 THERE WERE 9,703 Vehicles Enrolled
45% increase from July 2024 to July 2025
locator: Slide 'RUC Program Enrollment Growth' (data updated through July 2025)
context: Utah DOT describing its own program in a report to a legislative committee. The deck shows 9,166 of the enrolled vehicles are electric; the program became voluntary and EV-only in 2024.
note: Utah's per-mile rate was 1.25 cents in 2026 with an annual cap of $180, rising to 1.5 cents and $280 in 2027, indexed to consumer prices (UDOT program history page, not catalogued). Utah launched its program in 2020.

statement: Utah DOT projected for FY27, under current program parameters, that its road usage charge program would spend $668 thousand, 14.2% of its revenue.
anchor: FY27 Growth Scenario #1
RUC Expenses = $668K RUC Exp/Rev Ratio = 14.2%
locator: Slide 'FY27 Growth Scenario #1: Remove Payment Cap', first column (current program parameters)
context: A projection by the agency that runs the program, under assumptions in the deck (71,000 flat-fee customers, 23,000 per-mile customers, a $210 cap and a 1.47 cent rate); not a measured result. The text is a flattened slide, so the column assignment should be checked against the original slide.
note: Another Utah scenario in the same deck, with most electric vehicle owners on per-mile billing, gives 7.8% of revenue. The deck also reports a 66% cost reduction from FY24 to FY25 after a program redesign. Oregon DOT's roughly 0.3% for the fuel tax is EV-MOV-118; both states' figures show per-mile collection costing far more than fuel tax collection.

statement: Oregon's weight-mile tax applies to commercial vehicles over 26,000 pounds and is based on vehicle configuration and miles traveled on Oregon's public roads; it raised about $252 million in FY 2013, 15% of ODOT's revenues, from roughly 277,000 registered trucks.
anchor: responsible for registering commercial vehicles weighing more than 26,000 pounds, and administering Oregon's weight-mile tax
Proceeds from the weight-mile tax totaled approximately $252 million during FY 2013, or 15% of total revenues for ODOT.
Approximately 277,000 trucks are currently registered to operate in Oregon and are subject to the weight-mile tax.
The weight-mile tax is based on two factors: a vehicle's configuration and the miles traveled on public roads in Oregon.
locator: Background, 'The Motor Carrier Transportation Division administers Oregon's weight-mile tax for commercial motor carriers' (report p. 2)
context: Oregon Secretary of State's independent Audits Division, December 2013, in a report on a vendor pilot; used here only for its description of the tax and its FY2013 revenue, which is more than a decade old.
note: Statutory rates depend on declared weight and, above 80,000 pounds, on axles. Vermont's Agency of Transportation (January 2025, not catalogued) lists four states with weight-distance taxes on heavy trucks: Connecticut, New York, New Mexico and Oregon. ODOT's draft minutes (EV-MOV-118) put current collection cost near 11 percent.

statement: A 2021 study for Oregon DOT estimated weight-mile tax evasion in 2016-2018 at 8.63 to 11.33 percent of revenue collected using truck screening data, 8.13 to 10.66 percent using International Registration Plan filings, and 5.09 to 7.15 percent using International Fuel Tax Agreement returns.
anchor: average annual WMT evasion estimates ranging from 8.63 percent to 11.33 percent of total revenue collected from 2016 to 2018
potential WMT revenue evasion rates ranging from 8.13 to 10.66 percent
the minimum average annual revenue evasion rate was estimated to be 5.09 percent, and the maximum average annual revenue evasion rate was 7.15 percent
locator: Technical Report Documentation Page, abstract (item 16)
context: A university research team (Kentucky Transportation Center) under contract to ODOT Research Section, not peer reviewed; three methods that depend on matching vehicle screening, registration and fuel-tax records to tax returns. The authors prefer the screening-data method for its advantages (collected by ODOT rather than self-reported). The abstract box in the PDF extracts out of order, so the quoted wording is the same abstract as in TRB's TRID record 1888288.
note: No independent estimate of Oregon evasion was found, so this has no corroboration yet. The study says the previous measurement was more than 15 years earlier. Revenue and collection cost, not evasion, were the entries asked for on administration cost (EV-MOV-118).

statement: ITEP counted 26 states plus D.C. with variable-rate gas taxes in July 2025: 8 states with rates tied only to fuel prices and 18 states plus D.C. with rates connected to the cost of funding the network (typically inflation indexing), against 24 states with fixed-rate taxes.
anchor: Figure 1 highlights the 26 states, plus D.C., that levy variable-rate gas taxes.
a fixed-rate tax that does not change over time (as is done in 24 states today)
a variable-rate tax calculated as a percentage of fuel prices (8 states)
a variable-rate tax with some connection to the cost of funding the transportation network (18 states plus D.C.)
Typically, this takes the form of inflation indexing
locator: 'National Landscape of State Gas Tax Designs' (bulleted list and Figure 1)
context: ITEP is a tax policy think tank that favors indexing the gas tax; its counts of states are data, its preference for design is not evidence. Two of the 18 states (Nebraska, New Jersey) link rates to revenue or spending targets, not inflation.
note: NCSL reports the same 26 states and D.C. (EV-MOV-124). A January 2025 Vermont Agency of Transportation slide (not catalogued) counts a narrower 13 states that index their excise tax to CPI or a construction cost index, plus Colorado from 2032, and 10 states plus D.C. with price-based variable taxes; the count depends on how 'indexing' is defined.

statement: NCSL reports that, as of May 2025, 26 states and Washington, D.C. have a variable-rate gas tax that adjusts, to some degree, with inflation or prices without regular legislative action, and that 35 states and D.C. have enacted gas tax increases since 2013.
anchor: 26 states and Washington, D.C., have a variable-rate gas tax that adjusts, to some degree, with inflation or prices without regular legislative action.
Since 2013, 35 states and Washington, D.C., have enacted legislation to increase their state gas taxes.
locator: Introduction and 'Variable Rate Gas Taxes' summary (updated May 28, 2025)
context: NCSL is the bipartisan association of state legislatures; its count cites ITEP, so it confirms ITEP's list but is not an independent count. The same page lists the structure state by state (CPI, construction cost index, fuel prices, population, vehicle efficiency).
note: 'Variable-rate' here includes taxes that move with fuel prices, not only inflation indexing; the page's table shows which states index to CPI (for example Florida, Illinois, Rhode Island, Virginia, D.C.) or to a highway construction cost index (Alabama, Minnesota, Mississippi; Colorado from 2032-33).

statement: The Transit Costs Project, from a database of more than 900 projects in 59 countries, finds the United States is the sixth most expensive country in the world to build rapid-rail transit, and attributes the 8-to-12-times premium of New York's Second Avenue Subway over a composite low-cost baseline to physical structures, labor, and procurement and soft costs.
anchor: our database (Transit Costs Project n.d.) of more than 900 projects in 59 countries, including Hong Kong, the United States is the sixth most expensive country in the world to build rapid-rail transit infrastructure.
The five countries with greater average costs than the United States are building projects that are more than 65% tunneled.
Phase 1 of New York's Second Avenue Subway is 8 to 12 times more expensive than our composite baseline case.
The three primary factors are as follows: Physical Structures, Labor, and Procurement and Soft Costs.
locator: Transit Costs Study Final Report, overview: the paragraphs on the database and Figure 1, and on the three primary factors
context: A university research project (NYU Marron Institute) that argues for adopting low-cost countries' practices; its cost-driver multipliers come from case studies and its own estimates, and the authors say the New York premium range (8 to 12) is imprecise. The per-kilometer comparison is in a chart the text does not carry, so no per-kilometer figure is anchored; the text notes the US has only 37% of track tunneled, against more than 65% for the five costlier countries.
note: No independent source on US transit construction costs has been added yet; the International Union of Railways or a GAO report on New Starts costs could serve. Main causes named by the study: oversized stations (about 2 times the cost), lack of standardized design, labor use (40-60% of hard costs in the Northeast against 19-30% in low-cost cases), procurement culture and soft costs. The premium multipliers are the study's, not measured prices.

statement: FHWA's Proven Safety Countermeasures booklet states that converting a two-way stop-controlled intersection to a roundabout reduces fatal and injury crashes by 82% and converting a signalized intersection to a roundabout reduces them by 78%.
anchor: Two-Way Stop-Controlled Intersection to a Roundabout 82% reduction in fatal and injury crashes.
Signalized Intersection to a Roundabout 78% reduction in fatal and injury crashes.
locator: Roundabouts page of the booklet (Safety Benefits box; footnote cites the AASHTO Highway Safety Manual, 2010)
context: FHWA Office of Safety, booklet FHWA-SA-21 series, published 2021 under the Biden administration; an agency's own statement of effect sizes drawn from crash modification factors in the Highway Safety Manual, so graded as analysis. The percentages describe before-and-after changes at converted intersections, and applicability depends on site conditions.
note: Same publisher as the linked entry, so no independent corroboration yet; an independent evaluation (for example an Insurance Institute for Highway Safety roundabout study or the Highway Safety Manual itself) should be added before the dossier relies on it. FHWA's online page for roundabouts (highways.dot.gov) shows the same two percentages.

statement: FHWA states that a Road Diet (converting a four-lane undivided road to fewer lanes with a center turn lane) produces a crash reduction of 19 to 47 percent.
anchor: The resulting benefits include a crash reduction of 19 to 47 percent, reduced vehicle speed differential, improved mobility and access by all road users
locator: Road Diets (Roadway Reconfiguration) page, paragraph on resulting benefits
context: FHWA Office of Safety web page, undated, served in 2026 (second Trump administration site); an agency's own summary of earlier safety studies, graded analysis. The FHWA Road Diet Informational Guide's conclusion gives the same range as what practitioners can expect, depending on prior crash history, installation details and urban or rural setting.
note: Same publisher as the linked entry; no independent corroboration yet. The page's 'proven safety countermeasure' designation is FHWA's own.

statement: GAO's survey of 31 commuter rail systems found that 17 were still using federal COVID-19 relief funding in FY2023, that the relief laws let recipients spend it on a wide array of payroll and operating expenses, and that the systems' operating costs rose about 28 percent in nominal terms (9 percent after inflation) from FY2019 to FY2023.
anchor: Slightly more than half of systems (17) reported in our survey they were still using federal COVID-19 relief funding in FY 2023.
The laws gave recipients flexibilities to use the funding for a wide array of payroll and operating expenses
Across all 31 systems, operating costs increased about 28 percent in nominal terms, and 9 percent after adjusting for inflation.
operating costs increased from FY 2019 to FY 2023
locator: Introduction (relief laws' flexibilities) and the section on commuter rail funding (about pp. 19-20; footnote 28)
context: GAO, nonpartisan legislative-branch auditor (2025). It covers 31 commuter rail systems only, not transit generally, so it cannot be read as the national picture. Systems reported on their own relief use; 15 of the 22 that responded by February 2025 said they had spent all available relief funding.
note: No GAO report found that covers all transit agencies' use of the $69.5 billion; GAO-21-105202 (2021) reports 22 interviewed agencies used CARES grants for operating costs (not anchored). CRS gives the relief totals (EV-MOV-103). The ridership comparison in this GAO report for commuter rail is not used here.

statement: In the Mineta Transportation Institute's 2024 national survey (2,522 respondents), 74% supported raising the federal gas tax by 10 cents per gallon if the revenue were dedicated to maintenance (35% if spent for 'transportation' generally), 51% supported replacing the gas tax with a mileage fee whose rate varies with a vehicle's pollution, and 39% supported a flat-rate mileage fee on all travel.
anchor: A nationally representative sample of 2,522 respondents completed the online survey
74% of respondents supported increasing the federal gas tax by 10 cents per gallon if the revenue would be dedicated to maintenance.
only 35% supported the rate increase if the money were spent more generically "for transportation."
A majority of respondents (51%) supported replacing the gas tax with a mileage fee where the rate would vary according to the vehicle's pollution emissions
Support for this option was only 39%.
locator: Report abstract (sample size, 74%) and the research brief's 'Gas Taxes' and 'Mileage Fees' findings (35%, 51%, 39%)
context: University transportation institute's annual online survey (fifteenth year; February 7 to March 12, 2024); public opinion depends on the stated purpose and the fee design, as the authors stress. Support is for the tested wording, not an indication a vote would pass. The 2025 edition (EV-MOV-134) is newer.
note: Support for a flat-rate mileage fee rose from 22% in 2010 to 39% in 2024 and for the pollution-rate version from 33% to 51% (research brief). 64% supported lower mileage-fee rates for low-income drivers (press release; the report abstract says 62%). The Moving America project's link transweb.sjsu.edu/node/4576 resolves to the same report. The sixteenth-year survey (December 2025) is EV-MOV-134; use it for the latest figures.

statement: The European Court of Auditors found that the EU high-speed rail lines it audited cost on average 25 million euro per km (excluding tunnelling), that aggregate cost overruns were 5.7 billion euro at project level and 25.1 billion euro at line level (44% and 78%), that trains ran at only about 45% of design speed, and that three of seven completed lines carried far fewer passengers than the benchmark of nine million a year.
anchor: lines we audited cost 25 million euro per km (not taking into account the more expensive tunnelling projects)
Aggregate cost overruns for the lines and projects we audited were 5.7 billion euro at project level, and 25.1 billion euro at line level (44 % and 78 %, respectively).
trains run on average at only around 45 % of the line's design speed on the lines audited
on three of the seven completed high-speed lines we audited, the number of passengers carried was far lower.
locator: Executive summary, paragraphs VI and VII; main text on speed, passenger numbers and cost
context: An independent EU audit institution (2018), covering about 5,000 km of lines (about half the EU's high-speed network) in six member states, with data to 2016-2017; a skeptical audit that finds some very-high-speed lines were not needed, so it is evidence on cost-efficiency and not a verdict on high-speed rail in general. Costs are in euros as reported by the audited projects, not adjusted to US dollars or today's prices.
note: The same report finds the cost per minute of travel time saved ranges up to 369 million euro (Stuttgart-Munich), that four of ten lines exceed 100 million euro per minute saved, and that nine of 14 lines and connections lacked enough potential passengers. The 25 million euro per km excludes tunnelling, and the report says costs are rising. It is not a US comparison; no US high-speed rail cost per kilometer was added.

statement: CRFB, restating CBO's February 2026 baseline, says the Highway Trust Fund will run out of reserves in FY2028 and that the law then calls for spending to match revenue, which it estimates as a 40% immediate cut to highway spending.
anchor: CBO estimates the Highway Trust Fund will run out of reserves in FY 2028
The result would be a 40% immediate cut to highway spending
locator: Section 'Major Trust Funds Are Approaching Insolvency'
context: CRFB is a nonpartisan fiscal-policy advocacy group that favors deficit reduction and trust fund reform. Its insolvency year is CBO's, not its own projection; the 40% cut is CRFB's own estimate, and CBO's baseline assumes by statute that the fund keeps paying. A separate CRFB estimate (March 17, 2026, not anchored) puts the insolvency date at about July 2028 before any gas tax holiday. The Penn Wharton Budget Model was searched and no 2026 Highway Trust Fund projection by it was found.
note: Independent in publisher but not in method: it adds a read of consequences to CBO's numbers, so it corroborates EV-MOV-002 and EV-MOV-015 as a restatement, not as a second projection. A truly independent estimate of the fund's balance (for example Penn Wharton, Tax Foundation or a state DOT association) is still needed.

statement: FHWA's National Highway Construction Cost Index (2003 Q1 = 1) was 2.04 in 2021 Q2, reached 3.36 in 2024 Q3, was 3.31 in 2025 Q3 and was 3.13 in 2026 Q1.
context: FHWA Office of Transportation Policy Studies, second Trump administration; a measured price index built from the winning bid prices on state projects. Values are the portal's current vintage (data updated 2026-09-09) and are revised: Eno cites a peak of 3.3079 in 2025 Q3 (EV-MOV-133), against 3.3065 here.
note: Project arithmetic from the same series: 3.3065 / 2.0363 = 1.62, so costs were about 62% higher in 2025 Q3 than in 2021 Q2, and 2026 Q1 is about 54% above 2021 Q2. This is the index BTS used for EV-MOV-008, which reports a 63 percent rise across fiscal-year averages for FY2021-FY2025; the measure here is quarterly and on a calendar basis, so the figures differ slightly. The index is a price index for roadway construction, not total project cost.

statement: The Eno Center re-bases FHWA's cost index to April-June 2021 and finds the raw index has risen 58.8 percent to the October-December 2025 adjusted level, and estimates that rising costs cut the buying power of $270 billion in IIJA-era FHWA obligations by $87.6 billion, or 32 percent.
anchor: the raw cost index has risen 58.8 percent since that time (from a rebased 1.0000 to the October-December 2025 adjusted 1.5584).
in the April-June 2021, NHCCI had doubled to 2.0363
Under the IIJA to date, there have been $270 billion in such FHWA obligations (excluding the emergency relief program).
the total amount of obligations drops below $183 billion, a reduction of $87.6 billion, or 32 percent, of the buying power of the funding provided to FHWA by the IIJA to date.
locator: Article of July 2, 2026, paragraphs on the rebased index and the table of buying power
context: Eno is a nonpartisan transportation think tank. Its arithmetic uses FHWA's own index and FHWA obligations from usaspending.gov, so it is an independent calculation on the same data, not a second measure of costs. Eno's description mixes 'raw' and 'adjusted' values in the same sentence, which should be checked against its table.
note: Reaches the same 32 percent as BTS (EV-MOV-008) by a different base (April-June 2021) and a different spending base, so the match supports the order of magnitude, not the exact figure; the two should not be added together or treated as separate confirmations of one number.

statement: In the Mineta Transportation Institute's 2025 national survey (2,539 respondents), 75% supported raising the federal gas tax by 10 cents per gallon if the revenue were dedicated to maintenance, against 38% for the base case in which the money is spent 'for transportation'; 51% supported a mileage fee whose rate varies with a vehicle's pollution and 44% supported a flat-rate mileage fee.
anchor: A nationally representative sample of 2,539 respondents completed the online survey from February 3 to February 27, 2025.
75% of respondents supported increasing the federal gas tax by 10 cents per gallon if the revenue would be dedicated to maintenance
Only 38% supported the “base case” option presented, which was a 10¢-per-gallon gas tax increase.
A majority of respondents (51%) supported replacing the gas tax with a green-rate mileage fee where the rate would vary according to the vehicle’s pollution emissions.
only 44% supported a mileage fee with a flat rate for all drivers.
locator: Report abstract (sample size, 75%) and the year-16 research brief, 'Gas Tax Findings' and 'Mileage Fee Findings' (38%, 51%, 44%)
context: University transportation institute's annual online survey (sixteenth year; February 3 to 27, 2025), the latest edition found; public opinion depends on the stated purpose and fee design, as the authors stress. Support is for the tested wording, not a prediction of a vote. Same research team as the 2024 edition (EV-MOV-129), so the two are one series, not independent confirmation of each other. A 2026 edition may be due; I did not find one.
note: Compared with 2024 (EV-MOV-129): the maintenance-dedicated gas tax increase 74% to 75%, the base case 35% to 38%, the flat-rate mileage fee 39% to 44%, the pollution-rate fee 51% in both. The brief reports 63% support for lower mileage-fee rates for low-income drivers and 74% preference for paying a mileage fee in small installments.
